newsitem.title: INDIA: Move to open India insurance sector seen in budget.
newsitem.headline: Move to open India insurance sector seen in budget.

text.p: India's insurance watchdog said on Friday that fresh moves to open the sector to foreign private investors would be announced by Finance Minister P. Chidambaram when he presented his budget at the end of February.

The chairman of the Insurance Regulatory Authority, N.I. Rangachary, told a seminar in Bombay that Chidambaram would announce the steps at the end of February, when the budget for fiscal 1996-97 (April-March) is due.
"The Finance Minister has assured that he will make a statement along with his budget about the sequencing of the events he wants in the industry," Rangachary said.

India's insurance sector is dominated by two-state run monoliths, the Life Insurance Corp of India and the General Insurance Corp. But moves to open up the sector to foreign private investment have begun as part of a sweeping programme of free-market economic reforms launched in 1991.
Industry officials say the value of India's insurance sector is about 150 billion rupees ($4.4 bln) and the sector is growing at the rate of about 11 percent annually.
About 22 foreign firms from the U.S., Canada, Switzerland, Britain, Germany, the Middle East and Japan are gearing up to enter the insurance market.
Rangachary said that the Authority, which is still in a nascent stage, would hold the interests of consumers closest to its heart. "The industry requires a real cleaning-up," he said.
"We in the Authority are eager to inject into the system a procedure that would ensure the players do have a concern for the consumer," Rangachary added.
Rangachary said the IRA is determined to ensure that new insurance companies did not exploit political patronage in order to set up with inadequate capital.
The watchdog hoped to establish a procedure for the pricing of new insurance products that would require their vetting by an appointed actuary, Rangachary said.

"Such a system, which exists in the U.K. and the U.S., would place an obligation on the actuary to blow the whistle if the firm ignored his professional advice or persevered with products or pricing which are too unscientific," he added.
The IRA will not relax its rules on solvency margins, Rangachary said. "They will have to be adhered to, if any new player were to be admitted into this country, from day one."

The IRA also envisions for itself the role of an Insurance Ombudsman, initially holding the power to guide insurance companies in relation to consumer complaints, Rangachary said. He called for an efficient restructuring of the two Indian insurance giants, besides tight procedures to regulate appointments to the boards of new entrants.
